amostra.content:
Nobody runs a sub-3-hour marathon in week one.

And nobody builds an impressive marketing engine from scratch in month one (despite what your CEO hopes for).

I keep noticing how similar these two jobs are.

When you start marathon training, you don't have a base. You have legs, ambition, and a Strava account that's mostly empty. 

The new head of marketing walks in with the same thing: no pipeline, no attribution, and a CEO who wanted results yesterday.

Here's what both have taught me:

☝🏻 Base miles are boring. Do them anyway.

Easy runs build the engine. Positioning, ICP, and tracking build the marketing engine. Nobody claps for either.

✌🏻You can't sprint every day.

Run hard every day and you get hurt. Launch a new channel every week and nothing gets enough time (nor budget) to work.

🤟🏻 The long run is the whole point.

SEO, content, brand. Those are the 20+ milers of marketing. They feel slow until the day they carry you.

Your finish time is just the receipt of all the work you’ve been doing. So was your Q4 pipeline, sorry.

My marathon PR is 3:53. My goal is 2:55.

That gap doesn't close with one heroic workout. It closes with hundreds of quiet, unsexy ones.

Same with marketing.

Build the base, strengthen the base.

The speed shows up later.

The job hasn't changed. Earn trust. Now you're earning it from agents, too. 🤖

📏 Add continuous level to your magnetic level indicator without shutting down the process.

In sugarcane processing, the steam boiler sits at the heart of the facility. It drives the cane mills, the evaporators, the clarifiers and sometimes electrical generators. Some of these mills date back 100 years or more, and level control in the boiler is critical for safety, efficiency and profitability.

A sugar mill controlled water level in its steam drum with three differential pressure transmitters in two of three voting logic. The team wanted a second continuous level technology to serve as a redundancy to the DP cells, one they could integrate into the control system. The mill already had an SOR 1100 Series Magnetic Level Indicator installed as a redundant visual indicator to the sight glass required by boiler code.

SOR proposed the new SOR Measurement and Control 1310 Magnetostrictive Level Transmitter. The SOR 1310 uses the magnetic field from the float already inside the MLI to determine process level and outputs a 4-20 mA signal.

Installation took two people.

🔩 Mount the transmitter flush to the side of the MLI with two stainless steel hose clamps
🧱 Add an insulation pad to protect the transmitter from the 210°F process temperature
🔌 Make a two-wire hookup to the dual compartment housing on the transmitter head
🚫 Close no valves and shut down no process

The SOR 1310 started reading level as soon as it was wired. The control room set up the signal for operations to display. SOR asked the mill to trend the SOR 1310 against its DP cells. Over one week, both trend lines coincided, which showed the transmitter tracked boiler level correctly.

What the SOR 1310 brings to your level loop:
🎯 ±0.032 inch (±0.813 mm) accuracy, with measurement ranges up to 20 feet (6.1 m)
🔀 Top level and interface level measurement
📡 4-20 mA analog output with HART digital output
🔧 Quick-Cal function for simple recalibration
🖥️ Local LCD display
🧰 Non-ferrous mounts for easy installation or removal on an MLI, with direct insertion available for various tank applications
🛡️ Two year warranty

Think about the vessel where one level reading is not enough. A second continuous technology, installed without a shutdown, gives you a cross-check against your current loop.

Some of our team were at the Pinterest x Triple Whale Advertiser Summit last week - and a few things stuck.

People make 35,000 decisions a day. We're not competing for attention. We're competing inside an already-overwhelmed decision-making process.

That reframe matters for how we think about channels like Pinterest. It's a platform where users come to actively discover, save, and form intent - not passively consume. If you're only measuring who clicked last, you're crediting the closer and ignoring everyone who warmed the room.

The Triple Whale session reinforced something we believe deeply: better measurement isn't a reporting upgrade. It's a budget confidence tool. When you can see the full journey, you make better calls about where to spend.

Few things we're taking away:
- Creative is performance. Stopping the scroll is now a media metric.
- Last-click attribution actively misrepresents upper-funnel contribution
- Measurement clarity = scale confidence

Thanks to Julia Dolgodvorova, Bill Ready, Jeroen De Koninck, Natasa Tintor, Adam Saunders, Steven DSouza, Katie Lin, Patrick Falson and the broader Pinterest and Triple Whale teams for a genuinely useful session. Both partners doing strong work on closing the attribution gap for eCommerce 🙌

📏 Add continuous level to your magnetic level indicator without shutting down the process.

In sugarcane processing, the steam boiler sits at the heart of the facility. It drives the cane mills, the evaporators, the clarifiers and sometimes electrical generators. Some of these mills date back 100 years or more, and level control in the boiler is critical for safety, efficiency and profitability.

A sugar mill controlled water level in its steam drum with three differential pressure transmitters in two of three voting logic. The team wanted a second continuous level technology to serve as a redundancy to the DP cells, one they could integrate into the control system. The mill already had an SOR 1100 Series Magnetic Level Indicator installed as a redundant visual indicator to the sight glass required by boiler code.

SOR proposed the new SOR Measurement and Control 1310 Magnetostrictive Level Transmitter. The SOR 1310 uses the magnetic field from the float already inside the MLI to determine process level and outputs a 4-20 mA signal.

Installation took two people.

🔩 Mount the transmitter flush to the side of the MLI with two stainless steel hose clamps
🧱 Add an insulation pad to protect the transmitter from the 210°F process temperature
🔌 Make a two-wire hookup to the dual compartment housing on the transmitter head
🚫 Close no valves and shut down no process

The SOR 1310 started reading level as soon as it was wired. The control room set up the signal for operations to display. SOR asked the mill to trend the SOR 1310 against its DP cells. Over one week, both trend lines coincided, which showed the transmitter tracked boiler level correctly.

What the SOR 1310 brings to your level loop:
🎯 ±0.032 inch (±0.813 mm) accuracy, with measurement ranges up to 20 feet (6.1 m)
🔀 Top level and interface level measurement
📡 4-20 mA analog output with HART digital output
🔧 Quick-Cal function for simple recalibration
🖥️ Local LCD display
🧰 Non-ferrous mounts for easy installation or removal on an MLI, with direct insertion available for various tank applications
🛡️ Two year warranty

Think about the vessel where one level reading is not enough. A second continuous technology, installed without a shutdown, gives you a cross-check against your current loop.

Last week I was back at the Databricks Data + AI World Tour in NYC. It was my second year, and it was interesting to see how much the conversation has changed.
 
Last year most of the talk was about what AI could do. This year it was about whether you can trust what it tells you.
 
That came through most clearly in the hands-on Genie code workshop. We built a Genie agent on Lakehouse data so business users can ask questions in plain English and get answers on their own. Getting it to answer was the easy part. Getting it to answer correctly comes down to how well you've defined your business: your metrics, your terms, what "revenue" or "conversion" actually means at your company. Once that's grounded, the answers hold up.
 
If you've worked in analytics, you know how many hours go into reconciling two dashboards that show different numbers for the same thing. That's the problem this goes after.

The other session I was looking forward to was on agentic advertising, with panelists from 
Publicis Groupe, FOX Advertising, Horizon Media. Since I work in marketing analytics, this one hit close to home.
 
One example stuck with me. Media buying, even today, still runs heavily on phone calls and spreadsheets. On stage they walked through a buyer agent and a seller agent negotiating a real linear TV deal on Databricks. That's already happening.
 
What I appreciated more was how measured everyone was about it. Nobody was pitching "let the agents run everything." Publicis Groupe talked about deliberately holding agents back until governance, compliance and the ability to stop a campaign quickly are solved. FOX described a trust ladder I really liked: agents start as assistants doing the boring work, become coworkers once they're reliable, and only later become advisors. They advise people. They don't replace them.

My main takeaway: models are becoming a commodity. The teams that win will be the ones with clean, governed data and shared definitions underneath their AI.
 
I've been working on Databricks a lot more in my day-to-day lately, and this event made me even more sure that this is the direction I want to keep growing in.
 
Curious to hear from others: if you've tried Genie or built agents on your data, what was harder, the tech or getting everyone to agree on the definitions?

Spellbook CEO Scott Stevenson believes some of this month's major software outages aren't the result of hacks, but of companies rushing to patch vulnerabilities uncovered by their own AI agents:

"Every CEO I'm talking with is dealing with this. Every IT and engineering team is dealing with agents attacking the surface area of their app at a scale that they haven't seen before."

"Everyone is now running agents against themselves to find and fix vulnerabilities before others do."

"I think what is happening is people are running agents against themselves, finding reams of vulnerabilities very, very quickly and then having to patch them very quickly, and that's causing a lot of downtime."

A factory installs nine cameras.

Yet the biggest problem remains invisible.

The solution? Buy camera number ten.

But what if technology was never the real problem?

🎙️ This Wednesday, I'm going LIVE with André Oliveira, an engineer who worked on computer vision for autonomous cars in 2011/12 and later helped launch automotive production lines internationally.

We'll explore what self-driving cars can teach Plant Managers about Operational Excellence.

→ Are our sensors revealing problems or hiding them?

→ Can automation make a broken process look stable?

→ Who takes over when technology fails?

Cars learned to see. Have our plants?

📅 Wednesday, 25 November 2026

Join us for the conversation!

what an excellent example of the difference between collecting more data and actually understanding what those data reveal.
Your example of installing a tenth camera when nine have failed to identify the underlying problem illustrates an important limitation of automation.
Technology can improve visibility, but it cannot compensate for poorly defined processes, unclear responsibilities, or incorrect interpretation of the information collected.
Thank you for bringing this important discussion to your audience.
I would be interested to hear your perspective: when an automated system detects a recurring operational problem but management fails to act, how can organizations distinguish between a technological limitation and a failure of operational governance?

Interesting perspective! The biggest lesson from autonomous cars may be that better visibility doesn't automatically lead to better decisions. In manufacturing, even the most advanced sensors and automation cannot compensate for weak processes or unclear ownership. I'd ask André this: How do we ensure that technology helps operators identify and prevent problems rather than simply detect failures after they happen? Looking forward to the discussion!

I’d ask what the operators are still doing outside the system. The handwritten note, spreadsheet, extra walk to check something, or manual correction usually has a reason behind it. That’s where I’d spend some time before buying camera number ten.
What are the people experiencing that the cameras are not seeing?
Yes, . An engineer who has worked on both cars and production lines can share rare lessons. Looking at factories through the eyes of vision systems may show gaps that managers often miss.

Very interesting perspective, André.

In manufacturing, installing sensors and collecting data is only the first step. The real value comes when the information helps teams identify hidden problems, validate actual operating conditions and take timely corrective action.

Technology can make problems visible, but trained people and strong operating standards are what turn visibility into sustainable improvement.

A very relevant topic for today's manufacturing industry. Looking forward to the discussion!

Andre, the part I would ask about is how a car handles one sensor that disagrees with the others. I wonder who plays that role on a plant floor when camera nine and the operator see two different things.

O fim da IA fragmentada: Como escalar IA com segurança na sua operação

A adoção da Inteligência Artificial nas empresas está acontecendo de forma acelerada, mas muitas organizações estão enfrentando um novo desafio: o uso fragmentado de ferramentas, soluções e agentes de IA, sem uma visão centralizada de controle, segurança e governança.

Nesta edição do TDC Community Talks, vamos discutir a diferença entre as necessidades de quem está na operação, buscando produtividade e agilidade para resolver tarefas com IA, e as necessidades de quem lidera, que precisa garantir controle, auditoria, segurança e conformidade.

Com Theron Morato, Especialista de IA na Skyone, vamos explorar como superar a fragmentação da IA nas empresas, criando uma estratégia que permita escalar seu uso de forma segura, estruturada e sustentável, sem comprometer a autonomia e a produtividade dos times.
